title: PayPal Negotiates Sale to Stripe After Rejecting Initial $53 Billion Bid
excerpt: Stripe and private equity firm Advent International are discussing a higher price after PayPal deemed their July offer of $60.50 per share insufficient.
body:
• PayPal is in active negotiations to sell itself to Stripe and private equity firm Advent International, with the two sides discussing a price higher than the initial $60.50-per-share offer.
  • The July bid valued PayPal at roughly $53 billion, backed by approximately $50 billion in committed bank financing — but PayPal's board deemed the price insufficient.
  • A deal could come together in weeks, though no agreement is guaranteed. PayPal shares rose 1.8% to $61.66 after The Wall Street Journal reported the talks.
  • The potential acquisition would unite two of the world's largest digital payment platforms, which together processed $3.7 trillion in payments during 2025.

A $53 Billion Bid Rejected

PayPal Holdings is in talks to sell itself to a consortium of payments rival Stripe and private equity firm Advent International, according to people familiar with the matter cited by The Wall Street Journal. The two buyers submitted an offer of $60.50 per share in July, valuing the fintech pioneer at approximately $53 billion, but PayPal's board considered the price too low.

The two sides have since been negotiating a potentially higher price, with people briefed on the discussions saying a deal could materialize within weeks. There are no guarantees an agreement will be reached.

PayPal shares gained 1.8% to close at $61.66 on Friday after the Journal's report, giving the company a market value of about $54 billion. The stock remains a fraction of its pandemic-era peak above $300, when PayPal was valued at more than $280 billion.

From Pioneer to Takeover Target

The discussions mark a dramatic reversal for a company that helped invent digital payments and launched the careers of Elon Musk and Peter Thiel. Founded in 1998, acquired by eBay in 2002, and spun off as an independent company in 2015, PayPal rode the e-commerce boom to astronomical heights during the pandemic before a sharp decline set in.

"While some progress has been made in a number of areas over the last two years, the pace of change and execution was not in line with the Board's expectations."

— PayPal, in a statement accompanying its CEO transition

Competition from Apple Pay, Google Pay, and a host of buy-now-pay-later startups eroded PayPal's position. The company issued a profit warning in February, prompting the board to replace CEO Alex Chriss with former HP chief Enrique Lores in March. Lores has since reorganized the business into three distinct lines, cut costs, and accelerated AI adoption.

Recent results show tentative signs of recovery. Second-quarter revenue rose 5% to $8.68 billion, beating expectations. The company highlighted growth in its Venmo peer-to-peer payments platform, its Braintree payment processing unit, and its debit-card and buy-now-pay-later services.

Why Stripe Wants PayPal

The pairing is unusual: a payments technology powerhouse teaming with a private equity firm to acquire, not dismantle, one of fintech's original names. Stripe processed $1.9 trillion in payments in 2025, while PayPal handled roughly $1.8 trillion across its 440 million active accounts. Combined, the entities would control an enormous share of global digital payment flows.

Stripe's valuation climbed to $159 billion earlier this year. According to Reuters, the initial offer was backed by approximately $50 billion in committed bank financing — signaling a fully underwritten bid rather than an exploratory approach. Under the proposal, Stripe and Advent would hold equal stakes without plans to break up the company.

Both companies have also been building stablecoin infrastructure. PayPal launched its dollar-backed stablecoin PayPal USD in 2022, now worth about $4 billion. Stripe acquired blockchain startup Bridge for $1.1 billion in 2024 and is developing Tempo, a payments-focused blockchain.

What's Next

Dealmakers are weighing whether PayPal is worth more as a single entity or as a collection of assets, such as Venmo, that could be sold separately. The remaining spread between PayPal's trading price and the offer reflects the market's skepticism about regulatory clearance, board acceptance, and financing holding through protracted negotiations.

PayPal declined to comment on the talks. Stripe said it does not comment on rumors or speculation. Advent did not respond to requests for comment. If completed, the deal would rank among the largest technology acquisitions in history and reshape the global payments landscape for both consumers and merchants.
